claims.statement: When one forensic technique acquires unusually strong legitimacy, it becomes a benchmark that draws evaluation toward neighboring forensic occupations.

claims.statement: Institutional pathways shape how evaluative spillovers are encountered and acted on; locally immediate routes create a stronger impetus for local practice change than remote or nonurgent routes.

claims.statement: The technical compatibility between a benchmark technology and an occupation’s existing method shapes how feasible adaptation is, although compatibility by itself does not guarantee change.

claims.statement: Occupational values filter evaluative comparisons: alignment with valued ways of doing good work supports adaptation, whereas a threat to those values promotes resistance.

claims.statement: Occupations with greater professional authority are better positioned to resist technology-driven changes to their tasks.

claims.statement: Association with novel technology can raise an occupation’s symbolic legitimacy because technology is culturally linked to progress and rationality.

claims.statement: Differences in occupational work and field relationships generate distinct occupational cultures, including different values and preferred practices.

claims.statement: Changes in occupational practice are mediated by how workers make sense of institutional demands.

claims.statement: A benchmark technology is not interpreted as one fixed standard; neighboring occupations select different features of it when comparing the technology with their own work.
